title: X3 · Mystery: the order that vanished
description: A customer was told their order was saved. After a crash, it’s gone. Unlock the write path one step at a time, collect clues, and name the culprit.

problemStatement.overview:
**Case file #4417.** On Tuesday at **14:02:11**, a customer paid for `order:88213` and saw *“Order confirmed.”*

Half a second later, the orders node running **FastKV** (the team’s homegrown LSM store) was OOM-killed and restarted. When it came back, **order:88213 was gone**. Payments has the money; orders has no record.

You’re the detective. The board is locked. **Only one step is open at a time.** Place the right card on the glowing step to unlock it, and each unlock reveals a clue from the investigation.

A wrong card costs a heart. You have three.

When the whole path is open, you’ll name the culprit.
problemStatement.yourTask: Unlock all six steps of the write path, read the clues, and name the design shortcut that lost the order.
yourTaskSteps: Drop a card on the glowing step. A correct card locks in and reveals a clue.
Clues collect in the Story panel.
Once all six steps are open, answer: who’s the culprit?
hints: The clues are about FastKV specifically. Compare what it did with what the textbook step says.
One of the cards in the tray is the culprit itself.

platformSpec.kicker: Experiment X3 · Mystery room · Unlock one step at a time
platformSpec.passMessage: Case closed. FastKV said OK before the order was in the log.

finale.prompt: Name the culprit. Which shortcut lost order:88213?

options.label: Replying OK before the WAL write was on disk
A memtable limit that was too small
Deleting the WAL before the flush finished

finale.explanation: FastKV batches WAL writes every 1000 ms but acks as soon as the record is in memory. order:88213 was acked at 14:02:11.2, the last WAL batch covered up to 14:02:10.9, and the crash came before the next batch. Nothing was deleted early and nothing was ever flushed or compacted, so the record only ever lived in RAM.

pieces.title: Append to the WAL and fsync
pieces.blurb: The record is on disk before anything else happens.
pieces.clue: The WAL on disk ends at 14:02:10.9. order:88213 (14:02:11.2) is not in it.

pieces.title: Insert into the memtable
pieces.blurb: The record joins the in-memory sorted tree.
pieces.clue: The API log shows “200 OK order:88213” at 14:02:11.2. The client really was told it was saved.

pieces.title: Freeze the full memtable
pieces.blurb: At 64 MB it goes read-only and a fresh one takes writes.
pieces.clue: At crash time the memtable was only 22 MB. It was never frozen.

pieces.title: Flush it to a new SSTable
pieces.blurb: Written to disk in key order as an immutable file.
pieces.clue: No SSTable was written between 13:40 and the crash. The order only ever lived in memory.

pieces.title: Write a Bloom filter and index
Delete the WAL segment
pieces.blurb: Only after its memtable is safely in an SSTable.
pieces.clue: No WAL segments were deleted on Tuesday. Nothing was cleaned up too early.

pieces.title: Compaction merges SSTables
pieces.blurb: Background merge that keeps the newest version of each key.
pieces.clue: FastKV config: wal.sync = batch, wal.batch_interval = 1000ms, ack_on = memtable.

pieces.title: Reply OK first, write the log later
pieces.blurb: Ack once the record is in memory; batch the WAL write a second later.
pieces.trapIfPlaced: Suspicious. That’s not a step a safe write path takes. Keep it in mind for the end.

pieces.title: Overwrite the order’s page on disk
pieces.blurb: Find the page and write over it.
pieces.trapIfPlaced: That’s a B-tree move, not FastKV.

pieces.title: Flush every 1 MB instead of 64 MB
pieces.blurb: Smaller memtables mean data reaches disk sooner.
pieces.trapIfPlaced: Tuning, not a step. And the memtable was never full anyway.

pieces.title: Delete old versions from every SSTable
pieces.blurb: Edit each SSTable that holds the key.
